code.title: Pointer holds an address

followUps:
A pointer is as big as an address on your machine: 8 bytes on a 64-bit system, 4 bytes on a 32-bit one. It does not depend on the pointee type because the pointer only stores a box number, and every box number on the machine has the same width.

The pointee type matters only when you use the pointer: it sets how many bytes *p reads and how far p + 1 moves. So char*, double* and BigStruct* are all 8 bytes on 64-bit. (Pointers to member functions can be larger, often 16 bytes.)

A void* is a pointer to "some object, type forgotten". It can hold the address of any object, but you cannot dereference it or do arithmetic on it until you cast it back to the real type.

It is mainly for C-style generic interfaces: malloc returns one, memcpy takes two, and callbacks pass a user-data void*. Cast back with the type you stored, or the behaviour is undefined.

int n = 5;
void* v = &n;
int* back = static_cast<int*>(v);
std::cout << *back;   // 5

In modern C++ prefer templates, std::variant or std::any, which keep type safety.

code.title: Reference alias vs re-aimable pointer

followUps:
In a correct program, no: a reference must be bound to a real object, so it is never null. Trying to make one (int& r = *(int*)nullptr;) is already undefined behaviour, even before you read from it.

The compiler is allowed to assume &r != nullptr and may delete your null checks. If "no object" is a valid state, use a pointer, std::optional<T> or std::optional<std::reference_wrapper<T>> instead.

Because a reference cannot be re-seated, the compiler cannot generate operator=: assignment would copy the value into the referent, not rebind the reference, which is almost never what you want. So the implicit copy assignment is deleted.

struct S { int& r; };
int a = 1, b = 2;
S s1{a}, s2{b};
// s1 = s2;   // error: deleted
// would change a, not rebind r

Copy construction still works (it binds to the same object). Fix by using a pointer or std::reference_wrapper member, or by writing your own assignment.

The compiler usually implements a reference as a hidden pointer that is automatically dereferenced, but the standard does not say how, and the optimizer often removes it completely.

For a local alias like int& r = x; the compiler simply uses x directly, so there is no storage at all. For reference parameters and members, the address is passed in a register or stored in the object, so a reference member makes the class one pointer wider. Example: struct S { int& r; }; has sizeof 8 on 64-bit even though sizeof(int&) reports 4, the size of the referent.

code.title: The four const pointer forms

followUps:
Because the type system must stop you from sneaking a const object through a non-const door. The detailed example is in question 9: allowing int** to const int** lets you store the address of a const int into a plain int*.

The safe version is int** to const int* const*: add const at every level between the outer pointer and the thing that is const. Then nobody can write a const int* into the middle pointer.

Top-level const applies to the object itself (int* const p: p is const). Low-level const applies to what is pointed at (const int* p: the int is const). Copying a value ignores top-level const but must keep low-level const.

auto drops top-level const and references but keeps low-level const:

const int* const cp = &x;
auto a = cp;      // const int*  (top const dropped)
const auto b = cp; // const int* const

This is why auto x = cref; gives a plain copy, not a reference.

code.title: nullptr picks the pointer overload

followUps:
It is undefined behaviour: the C++ standard places no demands on what happens. On common desktop systems it usually crashes at once with a segmentation fault, because address 0 is not mapped.

But "usually" is not "always": on embedded devices address 0 can be valid memory, and optimizers may reason that the pointer was non-null and silently delete later null checks. Treat it as a bug, never as a reliable crash. Check if (p) where null is valid, and use sanitizers to find the rest.

Yes: delete nullptr; and delete[] nullptr; do nothing, so no check is needed before deleting. That is why "if (p) delete p;" is redundant.

It does not make a double delete safe: if p still holds the address of an already freed object, deleting again is undefined behaviour. Setting p = nullptr after delete makes a second delete of that same variable harmless, but not other copies of the pointer. Better to use unique_ptr and avoid manual delete.

code.title: Pointer arithmetic scales by element size

followUps:
*p++ uses the value then moves the pointer; (*p)++ increments the pointed-at value; *++p moves the pointer first, then reads.

Postfix ++ binds tighter than *. With int a[] = {10, 20, 30}; int* p = a;:

  • *p++ yields 10, p now at 20.
  • (*p)++ yields 10, a[0] becomes 11, p unchanged.
  • *++p yields 20, p now at 20.

The classic string copy loop while (*d++ = *s++); relies on the first form.

Because a[i] is defined as *(a + i), and addition is commutative, *(i + a) is the same thing, which is i[a]. So 2[a] and a[2] are the same element.

For int a[] = {10, 20, 30}; both a[2] and 2[a] are 30. It is a curiosity, not a style to use, and it only works for built-in pointers or arrays, not for overloaded operator[] on classes.

code.title: Array decay and where it stops

followUps:
a + 1 moves by one element; &a + 1 moves by the whole array. That is because a decays to int*, while &a has type int(*)[N], a pointer to the array.

For int a[10] on a machine with 4-byte ints, a + 1 is 4 bytes past the start; &a + 1 is 40 bytes past the start, the one-past-the-end address. That is a neat trick to get the end: *(&a + 1) as int*.

Because int[3][4] decays to int(*)[4], a pointer to a row of 4 ints, not to int*. A int** expects an array of pointers; a 2-D array is one flat block of 12 ints, with no pointers inside.

If you pass it as int** the code would treat integers as addresses and crash. Use int (*m)[4], a template taking int (&m)[R][C], std::array<std::array<int,4>,3>, or a flat std::vector<int> with index r * 4 + c.

code.title: Vector reallocation leaves old pointers dangling

followUps:
Because freeing memory does not erase it. The old bytes often stay in the heap or stack until something else reuses that space, so reading through the dangling pointer can still show the old value, and that is what makes the bug so dangerous.

Example: a function returns the address of a local int x = 5. Right after return the stack slot still holds 5, so the caller prints 5. After another function call overwrites that slot, you see garbage. It is undefined behaviour either way, and a different optimization level can change what you see.

No, it only fixes that one variable. Any other pointer, reference or iterator that points at the same object stays dangling, and the compiler cannot tell they are dead.

int* a = new int(5);
int* b = a;       // second pointer
delete a;
a = nullptr;     // a is safe now
*b = 1;           // b still dangles: UB

The real fix is clear ownership: one unique_ptr owns the object, others are non-owning, and weak_ptr where you must detect that the owner is gone.

code.title: Null, wild and dangling pointers

followUps:
The compiler can warn about some wild pointers (uninitialized use) and the simplest dangling cases, but it cannot catch null dereferences or most dangling in general.

Examples: -Wuninitialized and -Wmaybe-uninitialized flag some wild pointers. -Wreturn-local-addr catches returning the address of a local, and -Wdangling-pointer or clang's lifetime checks catch a few more. Null dereference is mostly found only when the null is obvious (-Wnull-dereference) because whether a pointer is null usually depends on runtime data.

Null: the program crashes with a segmentation fault, and a debugger shows the exact line; UBSan can check it with -fsanitize=null. Wild: AddressSanitizer reports invalid accesses, Valgrind reports use of uninitialized values, and MSan finds uninitialized reads in clang.

Dangling: AddressSanitizer reports heap-use-after-free and stack-use-after-return (detect_stack_use_after_scope), with the stack of where the memory was freed. Valgrind reports "invalid read" in the same cases. These tools slow the program, so run them in tests and CI.

code.title: Choosing how to pass parameters

followUps:
A const int& parameter is passed as a hidden pointer, so reading it needs an extra memory load, while an int by value sits in a register. For a small type the reference is therefore a little slower, not faster.

The reference can also stop the compiler from optimizing because it might alias other data, so it must reload after any write through another pointer. Rule of thumb: pass types up to about 2 machine words (16 bytes) that are trivially copyable by value; pass bigger or non-trivial types by const&.

Return a reference when the object outlives the call and the caller should act on the original, not a copy: for example a member accessor, operator[], or a chained operator like operator= returning *this.

class Box {
  std::string name_;
public:
  const std::string& name() const { return name_; }
};

Never return a reference to a local variable or a temporary: that is a dangling reference. If unsure, return by value; copy elision and moves make it cheap.

code.title: Safe const added at every level

followUps:
It is the same hole as array covariance: if Dog[] were accepted as Animal[] in Java or C#, you could store a Cat through the Animal view and break the real array. C++ closes the const version of it at compile time.

Both come down to one rule: a mutable container of T is not a container of a supertype of T. Read-only views (const int* const* here, IEnumerable<Animal> in C#) are safe, and that is covariance.

C is looser: it does not allow int** to const int** either, but it also rejects the safe int** to const int* const*, so the compiler only warns ("incompatible pointer type") and you often need a cast.

C++ added the multi-level qualification rule that makes the safe version legal with no cast. C23 improved some const rules, so check your compiler.

ASan typically slows a program about 2x and uses 2 to 3 times more memory, so it is for tests and CI, and rarely for production: it also adds attack surface and the extra memory costs. Some teams ship it in canary or staging builds.

For example a request that takes 100 ms might take 200 ms and 300 MB become 900 MB. Run it on the real test suite, fuzzers, and a pre-release soak test, and use lighter checks (hardened libstdc++ assertions, stack protectors) for production.

ARM MTE (Memory Tagging Extension) gives every 16-byte block of memory a small tag, and every pointer carries a matching tag in its top bits. If they do not match on a load or store, the CPU faults. That catches use-after-free and many buffer overflows in hardware with a small slowdown, so it can run in production.

Example: free memory is retagged, so an old pointer with the old tag crashes right away instead of silently reading new data. It is supported by recent ARM cores, Android and some Linux allocators, and detection is probabilistic, because with 4-bit tags there is about a 1 in 16 chance a wrong pointer matches by luck.

code.title: Arrow is (*p).x

followUps:
The pointer type has an overloaded operator-> that returns the raw pointer it holds, and the compiler then applies the built-in -> to it. So up->x becomes up.operator->()->x, which is (*raw).x.

T* operator->() const noexcept {
    return ptr_;   // the raw pointer inside
}

If the returned value is itself a class with operator->, the compiler repeats until it gets a real pointer. That is why smart pointers and iterators feel just like raw pointers.

A pointer to member names a field or method of a class without naming an object. You declare it as int Point::*m = &Point::y; and apply it to an object with .* or to a pointer with ->*.

Point pt{3, 4};
Point* p = &pt;
int Point::* m = &Point::y;
std::cout << pt.*m << p->*m;  // 4 4

It stores an offset (for data) or a function reference (for methods), not an address. Used for generic code that picks a field at runtime, such as std::invoke and std::mem_fn.

code.title: Which containers keep element addresses stable

followUps:
Because moving a vector's elements into a new buffer might throw halfway, and then the old buffer would be half destroyed, breaking push_back's strong exception guarantee. So std::move_if_noexcept moves only when the move constructor is noexcept.

Otherwise it copies, so if a copy throws, the old buffer is still intact and can be restored. This is why you should mark move constructors noexcept: a vector of 1000 strings moves in O(n) pointer steals, but a type with a throwing move gets 1000 deep copies on every growth.

Erase invalidates iterators and references at and after the erased position, because later elements shift one place left. Iterators before the erase point stay valid, and the capacity is unchanged.

For v = {10, 20, 30, 40} and it pointing at 20, v.erase(it) gives {10, 30, 40}; it now refers to 30 and the old end iterator is dead. Use the return value: it = v.erase(it);. For removing many items, use the erase-remove idiom or std::erase_if (C++20), which is O(n) rather than O(n squared).

The unique_ptr or shared_ptr hides the ownership, the raw pointer is then only an observer. The Core Guidelines' owner<T*> (from the GSL) is an alias for T* that marks "this raw pointer owns the object and must be deleted".

It is documentation plus a hook for static analysis, with no runtime cost. It is meant for old code and low-level types you cannot yet convert to smart pointers: owner<int*> p = new int; tells the reader and the checker that someone must call delete p.

Profiles are proposed sets of rules, enforced by compilers, that guarantee a safety property, such as type safety, bounds safety or lifetime safety, for code that opts in. The idea is that code is either checked and safe, or uses an explicit escape hatch.

Examples: the bounds profile would reject pointer arithmetic and require std::span indexing to be checked; the lifetime profile would diagnose returning a dangling pointer. They were proposed in WG21 as a route to memory safety without rewriting in a new language. Check the current status, since the design has been evolving.
